subject: math
title: Grade 3 Measuring Length, Mass and Capacity
seo_title: Grade 3 Measuring Length, Mass and Capacity Worksheets: Free Math Practice with Answer Key (BC Curriculum)
standard_text: Measurement, using standard units (linear, mass, and capacity)
meta_desc: Free Grade 3 math worksheets on measuring for the BC curriculum: centimetres, metres and kilometres, reading a ruler, grams and kilograms on a scale, millilitres and litres in a jug, and word problems. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: Choose the right unit, then read the marks carefully.
key_sub: On a ruler, start at 0 or subtract end − start. On a scale or jug, find what one mark is worth before you count. 1 m = 100 cm, 1 kg = 1000 g, 1 L = 1000 mL.
body_html:
Three things we measure

Length tells how long something is: centimetres (cm), metres (m) and kilometres (km). Mass tells how heavy something is: grams (g) and kilograms (kg). Capacity tells how much a container holds: millilitres (mL) and litres (L).

Key facts: 1 m = 100 cm, 1 km = 1000 m, 1 kg = 1000 g and 1 L = 1000 mL.

Benchmarks: know what 1 unit looks like

Compare with something you know. Then choose the unit and a sensible number.

UnitAbout the same as
1 centimetre (cm)the width of your fingertip
1 metre (m)a metre stick, or one big step
1 kilometre (km)a 15-minute walk
1 gram (g)a paper clip
1 kilogram (kg)a 1 L carton of milk
1 millilitre (mL)a few drops of water
1 litre (L)what a carton of milk holds

Measure with a ruler

Line up one end with 0. Read the number at the other end. If the object does not start at 0, subtract: end − start.

Read a scale or a measuring jug

Not every mark has a number. First find what one mark is worth: the jump between two numbers ÷ the number of spaces. Then count on from the number before.

Bigger is not always heavier

On a pan balance, the lower pan is heavier. A big object can be light.

Example

A ribbon is 1 m long. Liam cuts off 35 cm. How much is left?

Change to the same unit: 1 m = 100 cm. Then subtract: 100 − 35 = 65.

Answer: 65 cm

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Starting at 1 on the rulerStart at 0, or subtract: end − start
Counting the numbers, not the spacesFrom 0 to 6 there are 6 spaces: 6 cm
Counting every mark as 1 on a scale or jugFind what one mark is worth: jump ÷ spaces
Thinking a bigger object is heavierCheck with a balance: the lower pan is heavier
Thinking 1 kg is less than 900 gChange to the same unit: 1 kg = 1000 g
Leaving out the unitWrite cm, m, km, g, kg, mL or L after the number

faq.q: What do Grade 3 students learn about measurement in BC?
faq.a: In the Geometry and measurement area of the BC Grade 3 math curriculum, students measure with standard units: centimetres, metres and kilometres for length, grams and kilograms for mass, and millilitres and litres for capacity.

faq.q: What are good benchmarks for 1 cm, 1 m, 1 kg and 1 L?
faq.a: A fingertip is about 1 cm wide and one big step is about 1 m. A 1 L carton of milk holds 1 litre and has a mass of about 1 kg.

faq.q: Why does my child get the wrong length on a ruler?
faq.a: The most common mistakes are starting at 1, counting the numbers instead of the spaces, and reading the end number when the object does not start at 0. Ask your child to subtract: end − start.

faq.q: How can I practise measuring at home?
faq.a: Measure toys with a ruler, read the kitchen scale when you bake, and fill a measuring cup with water. Guess first, then check, and always say the unit.

items.q: Which unit is best to measure the length of a canoe?
items.e: A canoe is longer than a grown-up is tall, so use metres. Kilograms measure mass, not length.

items.q: Which unit is best to measure the width of a math notebook?
items.e: A notebook fits on your desk and on a ruler, so use centimetres. Kilograms measure mass, not length.

items.q: Which unit is best to measure the height of a cedar tree?
items.e: A cedar tree is very tall, but you can see the top. Use metres. Kilograms measure mass, not length.

items.q: Which unit is best to measure the distance from Kamloops to Kelowna?
items.e: Kamloops to Kelowna is a drive of a few hours, so use kilometres. Kilograms measure mass, not length.

items.q: Which unit is best to measure the length of a caterpillar?
items.e: A caterpillar is small enough to sit on your hand, so use centimetres. Kilograms measure mass, not length.

items.q: Which unit is best to measure the length of a crayon?
items.e: A crayon is short. It fits on a 30 cm ruler, so use centimetres. Kilograms measure mass, not length.

items.q: Which unit is best to measure the length of a soccer field?
items.e: You can run from one end of a soccer field to the other in less than a minute, so use metres. Kilograms measure mass, not length.

items.q: Which unit is best to measure the distance from Vancouver to Whistler?
items.e: Vancouver to Whistler is a long drive on the Sea-to-Sky Highway, so use kilometres. Kilograms measure mass, not length.

items.q: How many centimetres are in 1 metre?
items.e: A metre stick has 100 centimetres marked on it. So 1 m = 100 cm.

items.q: How many metres are in 1 kilometre?
items.e: Kilo means 1000. So 1 km = 1000 m.

items.q: Which list goes from the shortest unit to the longest unit?
items.e: A centimetre is the smallest. 100 cm make 1 m, and 1000 m make 1 km.

items.q: Choose the best estimate. Your fingertip is about ☐ wide.
items.e: The width of a fingertip is a good benchmark for 1 cm.

items.q: Choose the best estimate. One big step is about ☐ long.
items.e: A big step for a grown-up is about 1 m, the same as a metre stick.

items.q: Choose the best estimate. A classroom door is about ☐ tall.
items.e: A door is a bit taller than a grown-up. That is about 2 m. 2 cm is shorter than your finger.

items.q: Choose the best estimate. A new pencil is about ☐ long.
items.e: A new pencil fits on a 30 cm ruler, so it is about 19 cm. 190 cm is almost as tall as a door.

items.q: Choose the best estimate. A Grade 3 student is about ☐ tall.
items.e: Most Grade 3 students are a little more than 1 m tall. 130 cm fits. 13 cm is the size of a hand.

items.q: Choose the best estimate. A school bus is about ☐ long.
items.e: A school bus is about as long as 6 classroom doors lying end to end, so about 12 m.

items.q: Choose the best estimate. You can walk about ☐ in 15 minutes.
items.e: A 15-minute walk is a good benchmark for 1 km. You can walk 1 m in one big step.

items.q: Which is longer: 1 m or 90 cm?
items.e: 1 m = 100 cm. 100 cm is longer than 90 cm, so 1 m is longer. Do not just compare the numbers 1 and 90.

items.q: Which is longer: 1 km or 900 m?
items.e: 1 km = 1000 m. 1000 m is longer than 900 m, so 1 km is longer, even though 1 looks small.

items.q: How long is the pencil?
items.e: The pencil starts at 0 and ends at 6, so it is 6 cm long. Count the spaces, not the marks: there are 7 numbers from 0 to 6 but only 6 spaces.

items.q: How long is the eraser?
items.e: The eraser starts at 0 and ends at 4, so it is 4 cm long. Count the spaces, not the marks: there are 5 numbers from 0 to 4 but only 4 spaces.

items.q: How long is the piece of ribbon?
items.e: The piece of ribbon starts at 0 and ends at 9, so it is 9 cm long. Count the spaces, not the marks: there are 10 numbers from 0 to 9 but only 9 spaces.

items.q: How long is the crayon?
items.e: The crayon starts at 0 and ends at 7, so it is 7 cm long. Count the spaces, not the marks: there are 8 numbers from 0 to 7 but only 7 spaces.

items.q: How long is the crayon?
items.e: The crayon starts at 1, not at 0. So the end number is 1 too big: 6 − 1 = 5 cm. You can also count the spaces from 1 to 6: there are 5.

items.q: How long is the pencil?
items.e: The pencil starts at 1, not at 0. So the end number is 1 too big: 9 − 1 = 8 cm. You can also count the spaces from 1 to 9: there are 8.

items.q: How long is the eraser?
items.e: The eraser starts at 1, not at 0. So the end number is 1 too big: 5 − 1 = 4 cm. You can also count the spaces from 1 to 5: there are 4.

items.q: How long is the pencil?
items.e: The pencil starts at 2, not at 0. It ends at 9. 9 − 2 = 7, so it is 7 cm long. You can also count the spaces from 2 to 9: there are 7.

items.q: How long is the eraser?
items.e: The eraser starts at 3, not at 0. It ends at 7. 7 − 3 = 4, so it is 4 cm long. You can also count the spaces from 3 to 7: there are 4.

items.q: How long is the piece of ribbon?
items.e: The piece of ribbon starts at 2, not at 0. It ends at 8. 8 − 2 = 6, so it is 6 cm long. You can also count the spaces from 2 to 8: there are 6.

items.q: How long is the feather?
items.e: The feather starts at 3, not at 0. It ends at 11. 11 − 3 = 8, so it is 8 cm long. You can also count the spaces from 3 to 11: there are 8.

items.q: How long is the crayon?
items.e: The crayon starts at 4, not at 0. It ends at 10. 10 − 4 = 6, so it is 6 cm long. You can also count the spaces from 4 to 10: there are 6.

items.q: How long is the pencil?
items.e: The pencil starts at 5, not at 0. It ends at 12. 12 − 5 = 7, so it is 7 cm long. You can also count the spaces from 5 to 12: there are 7.

items.q: How long is the piece of ribbon?
items.e: The piece of ribbon starts at 3, not at 0. It ends at 12. 12 − 3 = 9, so it is 9 cm long. You can also count the spaces from 3 to 12: there are 9.

items.q: Leah measures a ribbon. It goes from 0 to 6 on the ruler. She counts the numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and says the ribbon is 7 cm. How long is it really?
items.e: Leah counted 7 numbers, but length is the number of spaces between them. From 0 to 6 there are 6 spaces, so the ribbon is 6 cm.

items.q: Noah puts one end of his crayon at 1 on the ruler, not at 0. The other end is at 10. How long is the crayon?
items.e: He started at 1, so the end number is 1 too big. 10 − 1 = 9 cm.

items.q: Sofia’s marker lies on a ruler. One end is at 4 cm and the other end is at 13 cm. How long is the marker?
items.e: It does not start at 0, so subtract: 13 − 4 = 9 cm. 17 cm adds the numbers instead.

items.q: Kai measures the classroom whiteboard with a metre stick. The stick fits along it exactly 3 times. How long is the whiteboard?
items.e: Each time the metre stick fits, that is 1 m. 3 times is 3 m.

items.q: A pencil is 15 cm long. A crayon is 9 cm long. How much longer is the pencil?
items.e: “How much longer” compares two lengths, so subtract: 15 − 9 = 6 cm.

items.q: Arjun lays 3 crayons end to end. Each crayon is 8 cm long. How long is the row?
items.e: 3 crayons of 8 cm: 8 + 8 + 8 = 3 × 8 = 24 cm.

sets.title: Read a scale in g and kg

items.q: How many grams are in 1 kilogram?
items.e: Kilo means 1000. So 1 kg = 1000 g.

items.q: The scale shows the mass of a bag of potatoes. What is the mass?
items.e: The numbers go up by 2 kg. There are 2 spaces between two numbers, so each mark is 2 ÷ 2 = 1 kg. The needle is 1 mark past 2: 2 + 1 = 3 kg.

items.q: The scale shows the mass of a pumpkin. What is the mass?
items.e: The numbers go up by 2 kg. There are 2 spaces between two numbers, so each mark is 2 ÷ 2 = 1 kg. The needle is 1 mark past 6: 6 + 1 = 7 kg.

items.q: The scale shows the mass of a box of apples. What is the mass?
items.e: The numbers go up by 2 kg. There are 2 spaces between two numbers, so each mark is 2 ÷ 2 = 1 kg. The needle is 1 mark past 4: 4 + 1 = 5 kg.

items.q: The scale shows the mass of a bag of dog food. What is the mass?
items.e: The numbers go up by 5 kg. There are 5 spaces between two numbers, so each mark is 5 ÷ 5 = 1 kg. The needle is 3 marks past 10: 10 + 3 = 13 kg.

items.q: The scale shows the mass of a box of library books. What is the mass?
items.e: The numbers go up by 5 kg. There are 5 spaces between two numbers, so each mark is 5 ÷ 5 = 1 kg. The needle is 3 marks past 15: 15 + 3 = 18 kg.
The numbers go up by 10 kg. There are 5 spaces between two numbers, so each mark is 10 ÷ 5 = 2 kg. The needle is 1 mark past 30: 30 + 2 = 32 kg.

items.q: The scale shows the mass of an apple. What is the mass?
items.e: The numbers go up by 100 g. There are 2 spaces between two numbers, so each mark is 100 ÷ 2 = 50 g. The needle is 1 mark past 100: 100 + 50 = 150 g.

items.q: The scale shows the mass of a box of crackers. What is the mass?
items.e: The numbers go up by 100 g. There are 2 spaces between two numbers, so each mark is 100 ÷ 2 = 50 g. The needle is 1 mark past 300: 300 + 50 = 350 g.
The numbers go up by 100 g. There are 5 spaces between two numbers, so each mark is 100 ÷ 5 = 20 g. The needle is 2 marks past 200: 200 + 40 = 240 g.
The numbers go up by 100 g. There are 5 spaces between two numbers, so each mark is 100 ÷ 5 = 20 g. The needle is 3 marks past 400: 400 + 60 = 460 g.
The numbers go up by 200 g. There are 4 spaces between two numbers, so each mark is 200 ÷ 4 = 50 g. The needle is 1 mark past 800: 800 + 50 = 850 g.
The numbers go up by 50 g. There are 5 spaces between two numbers, so each mark is 50 ÷ 5 = 10 g. The needle is 2 marks past 150: 150 + 20 = 170 g.

items.q: Look at the pan balance. Which object is heavier?
items.e: The left pan is lower. The lower pan holds the heavier object, so the bowling ball is heavier and the beach ball is lighter. The bigger object is not always heavier.

items.q: Look at the pan balance. Which object is heavier?
items.e: The right pan is lower. The lower pan holds the heavier object, so the brick is heavier and the pillow is lighter. The bigger object is not always heavier.

items.q: Look at the pan balance. Which object is lighter?
items.e: The left pan is lower. The lower pan holds the heavier object, so the rock is heavier and the bag of chips is lighter. The bigger object is not always heavier.

items.q: The pan balance is level. What is the mass of the jar of jam?
items.e: The pans are level, so the jar has the same mass as the weights: 200 + 100 + 50 = 350 g.

items.q: Which is heavier: 900 g or 1 kg?
items.e: 1 kg = 1000 g. 1000 g is more than 900 g, so 1 kg is heavier, even though 1 looks small.

items.q: The scale shows a bowl of blueberries. The empty bowl has a mass of 100 g. What is the mass of the blueberries?
items.e: Each mark is 50 g, so the needle is at 450 g. Take away the bowl: 450 − 100 = 350 g.

items.q: The scale shows some flour. How much more flour is needed to make 1000 g?
items.e: Each mark is 100 g, so the needle is at 600 g. 1000 − 600 = 400 g more.

sets.title: Read a measuring jug in mL and L

items.q: How many millilitres are in 1 litre?
items.e: 1000 millilitres fill 1 litre: 1 L = 1000 mL.

items.q: How much water is in the measuring jug?
items.e: The numbers go up by 200 mL. There are 2 spaces between two numbers, so each line is 200 ÷ 2 = 100 mL. The top of the water is 1 line above 200: 200 + 100 = 300 mL.

items.q: How much water is in the measuring jug?
items.e: The numbers go up by 200 mL. There are 2 spaces between two numbers, so each line is 200 ÷ 2 = 100 mL. The top of the water is 1 line above 600: 600 + 100 = 700 mL.

items.q: How much water is in the measuring jug?
items.e: The numbers go up by 500 mL. There are 2 spaces between two numbers, so each line is 500 ÷ 2 = 250 mL. The top of the water is 1 line up from the bottom: 250 mL.

items.q: How much apple juice is in the measuring jug?
items.e: The numbers go up by 500 mL. There are 2 spaces between two numbers, so each line is 500 ÷ 2 = 250 mL. The top of the apple juice is 1 line above 500: 500 + 250 = 750 mL.

items.q: How much water is in the measuring jug?
items.e: The numbers go up by 250 mL. There are 5 spaces between two numbers, so each line is 250 ÷ 5 = 50 mL. The top of the water is 4 lines above 250: 250 + 200 = 450 mL.

items.q: How much water is in the measuring jug?
items.e: The numbers go up by 250 mL. There are 5 spaces between two numbers, so each line is 250 ÷ 5 = 50 mL. The top of the water is 2 lines above 750: 750 + 100 = 850 mL.

items.q: How much apple juice is in the measuring jug?
items.e: The numbers go up by 100 mL. There are 2 spaces between two numbers, so each line is 100 ÷ 2 = 50 mL. The top of the apple juice is 1 line above 100: 100 + 50 = 150 mL.

items.q: How much water is in the measuring jug?
items.e: The numbers go up by 100 mL. There are 2 spaces between two numbers, so each line is 100 ÷ 2 = 50 mL. The top of the water is 1 line above 300: 300 + 50 = 350 mL.

items.q: How much water is in the measuring jug?
items.e: The numbers go up by 200 mL. There are 4 spaces between two numbers, so each line is 200 ÷ 4 = 50 mL. The top of the water is 1 line above 600: 600 + 50 = 650 mL.

items.q: How much water is in the measuring jug?
items.e: The numbers go up by 2 L. There are 2 spaces between two numbers, so each line is 2 ÷ 2 = 1 L. The top of the water is 1 line above 6: 6 + 1 = 7 L.

items.q: How much water is in the measuring jug?
items.e: The numbers go up by 2 L. There are 2 spaces between two numbers, so each line is 2 ÷ 2 = 1 L. The top of the water is 1 line above 2: 2 + 1 = 3 L.

items.q: How much water is in the measuring jug?
items.e: The numbers go up by 5 L. There are 5 spaces between two numbers, so each line is 5 ÷ 5 = 1 L. The top of the water is 3 lines above 10: 10 + 3 = 13 L.

items.q: How much water is in the measuring jug?
items.e: The numbers go up by 10 L. There are 2 spaces between two numbers, so each line is 10 ÷ 2 = 5 L. The top of the water is 1 line above 30: 30 + 5 = 35 L.

items.q: Which holds more: a 1 L carton of milk or a 750 mL bottle of water?
items.e: 1 L = 1000 mL. 1000 mL is more than 750 mL, so the carton holds more. Do not compare just the numbers 1 and 750.

items.q: Mei pours 500 mL of water into a tall, thin glass. Hana pours 500 mL into a short, wide bowl. Which has more water?
items.e: Both have 500 mL. The water in the tall glass looks higher, but the amount is the same.

items.q: Which tool is best for measuring 250 mL of milk for a recipe?
items.e: Capacity is measured with a measuring cup or a measuring jug. A scale measures mass.

items.q: How much more water is needed to fill the jug to 1000 mL?
items.e: Each line is 100 mL, so the water is at 400 mL. 1000 − 400 = 600 mL more.

items.q: Zara pours 250 mL of water out of the jug. How much water is left?
items.e: The water is at 800 mL. Water is poured out, so subtract: 800 − 250 = 550 mL.

items.q: The jug is filled to the top line, 10 L. How many more litres are needed?
items.e: Each line is 1 L, so the water is at 6 L. 10 − 6 = 4 L more.

sets.title: Choose the unit and solve word problems

items.q: Which unit is best for how much a water bottle holds?
items.e: A water bottle holds a small amount, so use millilitres. Grams measure mass.

items.q: Which unit is best for how much a bathtub holds?
items.e: A bathtub holds a lot of water, so use litres. Kilograms measure mass.

items.q: Which unit is best for the mass of a strawberry?
items.e: A strawberry is very light, so use grams. Millilitres measure capacity.

items.q: Which unit is best for the length of the Fraser River?
items.e: The Fraser River is very long. It flows across much of BC, so use kilometres.

items.q: Which unit is best for the mass of a salmon?
items.e: A salmon is heavy to hold up, so use kilograms. Litres measure capacity, and kilometres measure length.

items.q: Mei’s family drives 48 km to the BC Ferries terminal. After the ferry, they drive 36 km more. How far do they drive in all?
items.e: Put the two drives together: 48 + 36 = 84 km.

items.q: At the Terry Fox Run, Liam runs 5 km. His little brother walks 2 km. How much farther does Liam run?
items.e: “How much farther” compares two distances, so subtract: 5 − 2 = 3 km.

items.q: Sofia has a ribbon that is 1 m long. She cuts off 35 cm for a craft. How much ribbon is left?
items.e: 1 m = 100 cm. Cutting takes ribbon away: 100 − 35 = 65 cm.

items.q: A class plants 4 rows of beans in the school garden. Each row is 3 m long. How long are all the rows together?
Olivia rides her bike around a 400 m loop in the park. She rides 2 loops. How far does she ride?
A fisher catches 3 salmon. Each salmon has a mass of 4 kg. What is their total mass?
items.e: 3 salmon of 4 kg: 4 + 4 + 4 = 3 × 4 = 12 kg.

items.q: Leah’s hockey bag has a mass of 11 kg. She takes out her skates, which have a mass of 2 kg. What is the mass of the bag now?
items.e: Taking out the skates makes the bag lighter: 11 − 2 = 9 kg.

items.q: Zara picks 250 g of blueberries. Her sister picks 375 g. How many grams do they pick in all?
items.e: Put the masses together: 250 + 375 = 625 g.

items.q: A bag holds 1 kg of flour. A baker uses 350 g for bannock. How much flour is left?
items.e: 1 kg = 1000 g. Flour is used, so subtract: 1000 − 350 = 650 g.

items.q: It rains a lot in Vancouver. A rain barrel had 65 L of water. A storm added 28 L. How much water is in the barrel now?
items.e: Water came in, so add: 65 + 28 = 93 L.

items.q: Jasleen’s water bottle holds 600 mL. She drinks 175 mL at recess. How much water is left?
items.e: Drinking takes water away, so subtract: 600 − 175 = 425 mL.

items.q: Ethan packs 4 juice boxes for a field trip. Each juice box holds 200 mL. How much juice is that in all?
items.e: 4 equal groups of 200 mL: 4 × 200 = 800 mL.

items.q: On a camping trip on Vancouver Island, each camper drinks 2 L of water a day. How much water do 4 campers drink in a day?
items.e: 4 equal groups of 2 L: 4 × 2 = 8 L.

items.q: A watering can holds 5 L. How many full cans are needed to give the school garden 20 L of water?
items.e: How many 5 L cans make 20 L? 20 ÷ 5 = 4 cans.

items.q: A pancake recipe needs 500 mL of milk. Wei has 350 mL. How much more milk does he need?
items.e: Find the missing part: 500 − 350 = 150 mL.
